```{r setup}
library(llutils)
```

The examples below are small so they run quickly. llutils pays off at
100,000 elements or more, where its functions take milliseconds and base R
takes seconds.

## Coding free text with a keyword table

Free text often has to be sorted into categories: bank transactions into
spending categories, free-text medication fields into drugs, open survey
answers into codes. A keyword table does this, and `par_match_term()` looks
up the first keyword each string contains:

```{r}
transactions <- c(
  "SUPERMART 0412 ZURICH",
  "CITY FUEL STATION 22",
  "Streamflix monthly plan",
  "SUPERMART FUEL 0412",
  "Transfer to savings",
  "Mart & More 17",
  NA
)

keywords <- data.frame(
  keyword = c("supermart fuel", "fuel", "supermart", "streamflix", "mart"),
  category = c("transport", "transport", "groceries", "subscriptions", "groceries")
)

i <- par_match_term(
  transactions,
  keywords$keyword,
  ignore_case = TRUE,
  whole_word = TRUE
)
data.frame(transactions, category = keywords$category[i])
```

Three arguments make this work:

- **Order.** The first keyword in the table wins, wherever it occurs in the
  string. `"supermart fuel"` comes before `"supermart"`, so the fuel station
  at the supermarket counts as transport. Put specific keywords before
  general ones.
- **`whole_word = TRUE`.** Without it, `"mart"` would match inside
  `"SUPERMART"`, and a short keyword would turn up inside many longer
  words. With it, `"Mart & More"` still matches `"mart"`.
- **`ignore_case = TRUE`.** Statements mix `"SUPERMART"` and `"Supermart"`.
  This only folds ASCII letters; for other scripts, apply `tolower()` to
  both sides.

Rows with no keyword get `NA`, which shows what the table still misses:

```{r}
transactions[is.na(i) & !is.na(transactions)]
```

The same pattern works for:

- **Medication fields.** `"Aspirin 100mg 1x daily"` is matched against a
  list of drug names, longer names first (`"aspirin cardio"` before
  `"aspirin"`).
- **Open survey answers.** A codebook of keywords per code, such as
  `"commute"` and `"traffic"` for a transport code.
- **Literature screening.** Which drug, gene, or method from a list does each
  title or abstract name first?
- **Web logs.** User agents against a list of bot signatures. These are
  substrings of longer tokens (`"Googlebot/2.1"`), so leave `whole_word`
  off.

`par_match_term()` returns one term per string. That suits coding, where each
string gets one category. To keep only the strings that contain any term,
use `!is.na(par_match_term(x, terms))`.

## Filtering and validating with a regex

`par_detect()` is `grepl()` on all cores. It suits large text columns:

```{r}
log <- c(
  "2026-10-17 12:00:01 INFO request served",
  "2026-10-17 12:00:02 ERROR timeout after 30s",
  "2026-10-17 12:00:03 WARN slow query",
  "2026-10-17 12:00:04 ERROR disk full"
)
log[par_detect(log, " (ERROR|WARN) ")]
```

Validating identifiers works the same way. Here, rows whose ID doesn't have
two capital letters followed by six digits:

```{r}
id <- c("CH123456", "DE654321", "ch123456", "FR12345")
id[!par_detect(id, "^[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{6}$")]
```

To find which of many literal terms appear, an alternation such as
`"aspirin|ibuprofen|paracetamol"` is fast in `par_detect()`: Rust's regex
engine searches all of its branches at once. For a case-insensitive search
over many terms, use `par_match_term(ignore_case = TRUE)` instead: `(?i)`
makes a large alternation slow.

Factor columns are matched by their levels, so a factor of a million
elements with 50 levels costs little more than matching 50 strings.

## Lookups and joins

`par_match()` and `%par_in%` return exactly what `match()` and `%in%`
return, so they can replace them anywhere. Some common uses:

```{r}
orders <- data.frame(
  customer = c(101L, 205L, 101L, 999L),
  amount = c(20, 35, 12, 8)
)
customers <- data.frame(
  id = c(101L, 205L, 307L),
  region = c("north", "south", "east")
)

# Bring in a column from another table, as a left join would
orders$region <- customers$region[par_match(orders$customer, customers$id)]
orders

# Keep the rows whose key is in a set
orders[orders$customer %par_in% c(101L, 307L), ]

# Check that every order has a known customer
all(orders$customer %par_in% customers$id)
```

Matching a vector against itself gives the position of each element's first
occurrence, so it also finds duplicates:

```{r}
x <- c("a", "b", "a", "c", "b")
first <- par_match(x, x)
first
first != seq_along(x) # same as duplicated(x)
```
